summary.text:
Paper set is a one-page covering report (1410) whose figures all sit in the companion 17-page appendix (1406). Read together. The cover's unique contribution is a named author with an email address — Steve Freeman, Chief Finance Officer (Deputy Chief Executive) — which the appendix does not carry.

The book is highly front-loaded. £77.975m of debt (62.7%) rolls inside twelve months against a total of £124.413m at 24.3.2026. Half of the book (£65m of £124m) is fixed-term borrowing from other local authorities; the other half (£59.413m) is PWLB. On the paper's own words (9.8): 'he continues to investigate other sources of finance, such as local authority loans and bank loans, that may be available at more favourable rates.' A live disclosure that the PCC is looking beyond PWLB for the next round of long-term borrowing.

The CFR trajectory is the other half of the story. £122.057m at 31/3/2026 becomes £270.050m by 31/3/2029 — +£148m in three years, +121%. External borrowing on its current maturity profile drops to £32.288m over the same period. The combined borrowing requirement is £237.762m by 31/3/2029, with £107.255m of that in the twelve months to 31/3/2027 alone. The interest budget in the same table rises £5.893m to £14.584m — 2.5x in three years.

Our balance-sheet identity ties to every year-end printed (no OLTL adjustment). The loan-book reconciliation does not tie — we hold 4 PWLB loans for £24.013m against the paper's £59.413m at 24.3.2026, a coverage gap of about £35m. Recorded on our file, kept out of the email.

officer.body:
Hi Steve,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every borrower's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, the inter-LA lending market, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council and every PCC in the country, so we can see how a body's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a couple of thoughts on the 2026/27 strategy that went to JIAC on 1 June. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The strategy is clearly laid out and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The first thing that struck us is the pair of numbers your paragraph 9.4 puts side by side. 62.7% of the debt book — £77.975m of £124.413m — matures inside twelve months from 1 April. Then paragraph 7.3 has the CFR going from £122.057m to £176.049m over the same twelve months, and the borrowing/(investment) need row shows £107.255m for 2026/27 alone, rising to £237.762m over the three-year forecast. Some of that number overlaps the maturities (the CFR table assumes about £58m of the current book runs off in 2026/27 against the £77.975m in the under-1-year bucket) but between the refinancing lump and the CFR growth it is a very concentrated window of PWLB and inter-authority decisions for a book that today sits at £124m.

Your paragraph 14.1 has priced that assumption. Net capital financing cost budget rises from £6.391m in 2026/27 to £17.062m by 2029/30, with interest payable alone going £5.893m to £14.584m — a 2.5x increase in three years. The bit of that figure that is worth checking is the interest receivable line, held at −£2.000m every year. On the trajectory in 7.3 the investment balance should fall as the CFR is externalised, so the flat receivable figure is a modelling choice worth being explicit about with members.

What we can genuinely offer here connects to your paragraph 9.8: 'he continues to investigate other sources of finance, such as local authority loans and bank loans, that may be available at more favourable rates.' Half the current book — £65m of £124m — is already fixed-term borrowing from other authorities, so this is a continuation of an existing strategy rather than a new one, and it is the market nobody publishes. Every body sees the trades it does, none sees the distribution across the sector. We track it daily — what other authorities are actually paying for one-, three-, six- and twelve-month LA-to-LA money — and where the deep tenors reach. For scale on the PWLB side, July's activity was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, and PWLB 10-year certainty is sitting around 5.63% on today's fixing against the 4.30–4.35 10-year gilt central case in your Arlingclose table on page 5. The monthly breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

One standing note. CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates put the liability benchmark in front of every member. Yours is drawn on page 8 and paragraph 8.2 already says 'consideration will be given to undertake some long-term borrowing in the next few years' — the chart shows net loans requirement peaking around £340m in 2030–2032 against £124m of external borrowing today. That gap is the number a member will ask about. We hold an interactive version fed by live rates so the shape moves as the market does.

One small disclosure. Our PWLB file for the PCC is not currently the full book — we hold fewer loans than your table on page 6 shows for 24 March, so we've kept the loan-level reconciliation out of this email rather than quote a figure we cannot yet stand behind. That is our data to fix rather than yours, but it is honest to say so.

On training, four fit the position the strategy describes. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets goes to where half your book already sits and where paragraph 9.8 is pointing. PWLB drawdown mechanics — certainty vs standard rate matters if the balance shifts back toward PWLB. Liability benchmark — reading it and setting one goes to page 8. And DMADF deep dive goes to the £52.785m that sits there today at 3.70%. All 115 courses are free to local authorities and PCCs until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 (covering report 1410 and Appendix A 1406), Joint Independent Audit Committee, 1 June 2026.
